body.text: The Philippines has been forceful in asserting its territorial claims in the South China Sea, at times resorting to legal means. In response to its escalating confrontation with China over these claims, Manila has deepened defense cooperation with its treaty ally, the United States. In adopting a foreign and security policy anchored in the U.S. alliance within the framework of U.S.-China rivalry, the Philippines stands apart from other ASEAN member states.

This July also marked the tenth anniversary of the South China Sea Arbitral Tribunal Award issued by the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in 2016, a case originally brought by the Philippines. Fourteen countries, including the Philippines, issued a joint statement reaffirming the award’s legal binding force. The other ASEAN states, however, did not join that statement.

Skirmishes between the Philippines and China have also been frequent: disputes over the drawing of baselines around Scarborough Shoal, and harassment by coast guard vessels and naval ships near Second Thomas Shoal, among other incidents. In June, China imposed sanctions on Philippine Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro and members of his immediate family, and during a telephone conversation this November, Beijing also criticized the conduct of a number of Philippine politicians. The gap between the Philippines and other ASEAN members in terms of their distance from China over the South China Sea issue appears to be widening.

That said, it should be noted that other ASEAN claimant states have also experienced their own friction with China. In March of this year, Vietnam protested China’s land reclamation and facility construction in the Paracel Islands, demanding an immediate halt. Malaysia, too, announced that it was monitoring Chinese Coast Guard (CCG) vessels transiting within its exclusive economic zone (EEZ) off Sarawak, and stated that it would continue to maintain its own presence in those waters. While there are differences in how these countries respond to the PCA arbitration award, all of them have experienced various forms of friction with China as positions remain at an impasse.

The deepening of ties between the Philippines and Vietnam is also worth noting. In June, Vietnamese President To Lam visited Manila and elevated the relationship to an “Enhanced Strategic Partnership,” signing a memorandum on defense cooperation. Vietnam did not join the joint statement marking the tenth anniversary of the PCA arbitration award, but on the same day the statement was issued, it released its own separate statement calling for a peaceful resolution in conformity with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). This has been interpreted as an implicit endorsement of the PCA arbitration award.

In other words, while the U.S.-Philippines alliance does set the Philippines apart within ASEAN, the Philippines and the other South China Sea claimant states are hardly at opposite extremes on the issue. Moreover, the Philippines has avoided aggressively pressing its own positions on the South China Sea within ASEAN forums, prioritizing its role as a consensus-builder when it holds the chair. The South China Sea section of the Joint Communiqué of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in July 2026 showed almost no change in wording from the previous year.

Even as tensions have deepened, China and the Philippines also appear to be avoiding a decisive deterioration in the relationship. As 2026 has progressed, skirmishes have continued, but so has the search for de-escalation, through resumed dialogue, foreign ministers’ meetings, and telephone diplomacy. It is also worth noting that China’s sanctions on the defense minister were directed at an individual rather than at the Philippines as a whole. This can be read as a strategy to exploit divisions within the Philippines over China policy, but it can equally be interpreted as aimed at avoiding further escalation between the two countries.

The Philippines, in short, is not entirely aligned with the West. It is raising tensions with China while avoiding a decisive rupture. And while at a slower pace than other ASEAN states, the Philippines is itself becoming integrated into Chinese-centered supply chain networks. The historical precedents of the Arroyo and Duterte administrations make clear that a government more oriented toward economic ties with China could well produce shifts in China policy.

Defense cooperation between the Philippines and Japan has been strengthening since the first 2+2 meeting in April 2022, through the entry into force of the Japan-Philippines Reciprocal Access Agreement (RAA), bilateral and multilateral joint exercises, capacity-building assistance, and the transfer of defense equipment and technology. For the Philippines, this is part of an effort to secure its own defense by reinforcing partnerships beyond the United States. Nonetheless, the Philippines maintains its channels to China and retains room for flexible policy adjustments in the future. This is a subtly different position from Japan’s, which is struggling even to resume a substantive dialogue with China. If the Philippines-Japan win-win relationship is to be made sustainable, both sides will need the composure to discern clearly where their positions converge and where they differ.
